t: Spreadsheets 2: IF, VLOOKUP, validation, templates, modelling, charts and macros
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L12: Spreadsheets 2: IF, VLOOKUP, validation, templates, modelling, charts and macros.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Write IF, nested IF and VLOOKUP functions and explain what each part does. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Beyond simple sums, spreadsheets have features that make decisions, find information, check input and save repeated work. The IF function tests a condition and returns one result when it is true and another when it is false, so a sheet can show Pass or Fail, add a delivery charge, or choose between two exchange rates on its own. VLOOKUP searches the first column of a lookup table and returns matching information, such as a price, from the same row. Conditional formatting changes how a cell looks when a condition is met, so important values stand out.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Data validation limits what can be typed into a cell, and an error alert asks the user to try again. Templates give a ready-made layout, and importing brings in data from other software without retyping. Spreadsheets can also be used as models to answer what-if questions, charts show results visually, and macros automate tasks that are done again and again. Each feature saves time, reduces errors or makes information easier to understand.
Right. What else do we need to know?

An IF function has three parts inside its brackets, separated by commas: the condition, the value if true and the value if false. the formula on screen shows Pass for 50 or more. Text results need double quotation marks; numbers, cell references and calculations do not, so the formula on screen gives free delivery on larger orders and otherwise uses the charge in K1. Read operators carefully: greater than means greater than, so a value equal to the boundary gives the false result. A nested IF places a second IF in the false part of the first, giving three possible results, such as Distinction, Merit or Fail.
Got it. Keep going.

Test the highest boundary first and close every bracket. VLOOKUP has four parts: the value to look for, the table range, the column number to return from, and FALSE for an exact match. If the value is not in the first column of the table, the result is #N/A. The table range is usually absolute, such as G20 with dollar signs:I24 with dollar signs, so that the formula can be replicated down a column without the table moving.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Conditional formatting applies a format, such as a red fill or bold font, only to cells that meet a rule. Because the rule is applied automatically, the formatting changes when the data changes, which is more reliable than colouring cells by hand. Data validation controls input at the point of entry. A range check might allow only whole numbers from 1 to 16; a list check gives a drop-down of allowed values, which is quicker and avoids spelling mistakes. An input message can explain what to enter, and an error alert pops up if invalid data is typed.
Okay. Keep going.

Validation can only check that data is sensible, not that it is correct. A template is a pre-designed workbook with headings, formatting, formulae and validation already in place, so other people only add their data. Protecting the formula cells stops users breaking them. Importing uses a wizard to bring in data from a database table, text file or web page; the file may need to be in CSV format first.
Go on.

A spreadsheet model represents a real situation with input values and formulae that act as rules. Changing an input, such as a price, makes every dependent formula recalculate, so the user can see the effect straight away. This is what-if analysis. In a sports camp model, raising the price from 35 pounds to 38 pounds but losing 15 bookings changes profit from 540 pounds to 600 pounds, which helps the organiser decide. Models let managers test many options quickly, cheaply and without risk, but the predictions are only as reliable as the data and rules used.
Right. Keep going.

Charts make results easier to understand at a glance and to show in presentations. Choose the type to suit the data: column or bar to compare categories, line for trends over time, pie for parts of a whole. A good chart has a title, axis titles with units and a legend when there is more than one data series. A macro records a sequence of actions so it can be replayed with one click, saving time and making sure repeated tasks are done the same way every time.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
IF function?
A function that tests a condition and returns one value if it is true and another if it is false, e dot g. the formula on screen.
Nested IF?
An IF function placed inside another IF function so that more than two outcomes are possible, e dot g. the formula on screen.
VLOOKUP?
Vertical lookup: a function that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from a specified column in the same row. It updates automatically if the source data changes.
Lookup table?
The range of cells searched by VLOOKUP; the values to be matched are in its first column.
Conditional formatting?
Formatting (e dot g. fill or font colour) that is applied automatically to cells only when a specified condition is met, e dot g. hours worked over 40 highlighted.
Data validation?
An automatic check when data is entered that it is sensible and within acceptable limits, e dot g. a range check of 1 to 16. It cannot check the data is correct.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

IF questions appear almost every year. Marks are given for the function name, a correct condition, both results in the right order and correct punctuation, so write the whole formula, including the equals sign, commas and quotation marks around text. Nested IF has been asked for three results, and 2025 combined IF with an absolute reference. VLOOKUP appears as a multiple-choice question and as an explain question. Examiners reported weak answers, so learn to explain each part: what is looked up, where it is searched for, which column is returned and why FALSE is used. Chart questions ask for the cell ranges used and the best chart type with a reason. Templates, validation and macros and what-if modelling need a clear description plus a benefit linked to the scenario.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. In the formula on screen, what does the 2 tell the spreadsheet? Is it A, Which column of the table to search; B, How many rows to check; C, Which column of the table to return a value from; D, Where to put the answer?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: Which column of the table to return a value from. VLOOKUP always searches the first column; the column number says which column the answer comes from.
